summary:
Altai Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources record no regional deviation: the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care, the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" statutes apply in full to a visitor in this region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment updated 11 June 2025) sets out the baseline a trans visitor here faces. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. No legislation prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment.

A document presenting a gender marker that does not match the traveller's presentation therefore carries direct exposure at any checkpoint, hotel registration or police stop, because the legal change that would reconcile it is unavailable.

Publicly promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence punishable by fines or detention of up to 15 days, and repeat offences can be prosecuted criminally with penalties of up to four years' imprisonment. The 2023 extremist designation criminalises support for or activity within the designated movement.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, about 98 of them administrative. Since January 2024, 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation: one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or of unknown outcome.

On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an "extremist organisation" over the sale of fiction exploring LGBT themes; the charge carries up to 12 years in prison.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia, which covers Altai Krai, advises against all travel and states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported. The advisory identifies displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, as a crime.

The UK Home Office note records that at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office assessment holds that LGB people generally face no real risk of state persecution on the basis of orientation alone, with the exception of the North Caucasus, a zone that does not include Altai Krai. That assessment is drawn on orientation grounds and does not offset the gender-identity provisions, which ban transition outright.

The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims.

Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity. The national conviction and case totals recorded by Human Rights Watch apply equally in Altai Krai, where the sources document no specific case; the absence of a local case is not evidence of local non-enforcement, since the charges at issue are brought under national statutes.

The reach of the extremist designation now extends beyond bars and public display into publishing and commercial activity, as the article 282.2 charges against publishing-house staff show.

The US State Department advisory advises against all travel to Russia, a blanket warning that sits above and alongside the LGBT-specific detention and deportation exposure.
localsOnly:
Trans people in Russia cannot adopt or foster children, and gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, so the mismatch between a resident's presentation and their papers is permanent under current law.

No legislation prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment, leaving residents without a domestic legal remedy in the settings where they live and work.

Publicly promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence carrying fines or detention of up to 15 days; a repeat offence can be prosecuted as a criminal matter with up to four years' imprisonment.

Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, ending legal access to gender-affirming care for residents as well as visitors.

The UK Home Office note records that at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents a specific enforcement case, raid or prosecution within Altai Krai itself; the conviction and case figures cited are national totals.

The inventory does not address regional police or prosecutor practice in Altai Krai, regional interior-ministry statements on the extremist designation, or any local ordinance on public expression.

Entry screening, border checks and document inspection at Altai Krai's airports and land crossings are not covered by the sources; the document-mismatch exposure described in the summary is inferred from the national ban on gender-marker change, not from a documented local screening procedure.

Local availability of legal name-change services, competent legal representation, or any affirming healthcare provider within Altai Krai is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The documented case of a transgender woman held in a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk concerns a facility outside this region and is not evidence of conditions in Altai Krai.
